The little ground tyrant (Syrtidicola fluviatilis) is a small passerine inhabiting riparian zones of southern South America, and its life history traits have been documented through field studies and captive observations. Newly hatched chicks emerge from eggs incubated at 32 °C [T = 32 °C] after a developmental period of approximately 15.5 days [ab = approximately 15.5 days], a duration consistent with that of other small tyrannids. At the moment of hatching, the neonatal body mass is remarkably low, with the initial wet weight measuring only 1.6 grams [Ww0 = 1.6 grams]; this altricial state demands intensive parental provisioning during the early nestling phase. The downy chicks are brooded continuously for the first several days, relying entirely on the parents for thermoregulation and food delivery. During this period, the young grow rapidly, their body mass increasing several-fold as they convert the arthropod prey brought by both adults into somatic tissue. The nestlings remain in the cup-shaped nest, hidden among dense emergent vegetation, until they reach the developmental stage at which flight feathers have sufficiently emerged, a milestone that marks the transition to the fledgling stage.

Under the thermal regime characteristic of this species' active metabolic periods, specifically at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the developmental schedule proceeds along a predictable timeline. The fledging stage, defined as the moment when the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and departs the nest, occurs at 16 days after hatching [tx = 16 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This comparatively early nest departure is typical of many open-cup nesting passerines that face high predation risk during the nestling phase, pushing the young toward an earlier but riskier independence. Following nest departure, the fledgling remains dependent on its parents for food and protection for a further period, during which it refines its foraging skills and flight capabilities. The post-fledging phase is a critical bottleneck in the life cycle, as mortality rates are highest during this transition from parental care to full self-sufficiency. The brevity of the nestling period reflects a trade-off between the benefits of extended growth in the nest and the imperative to escape from a vulnerable location.

The same thermal conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] govern the subsequent maturation process, as the species progresses through its juvenile and sub-adult phases toward reproductive competence. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal development and the capacity to breed, is attained at 48 days after hatching [tp = 48 days after hatching], a relatively rapid maturation rate for a Neotropical passerine of this body size at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This early sexual maturation is likely an adaptive response to the high adult mortality rates typical of small birds in open habitats, favoring individuals that can reproduce quickly rather than delaying breeding to invest in somatic growth. The juvenile bird gradually molts into adult plumage during this period, and behavioral observations indicate that young males begin to establish foraging territories well before they are physiologically capable of breeding. The development of the reproductive organs is accompanied by hormonal shifts that drive the transition from the sub-adult to the fully mature state, preparing the individual for its first breeding attempt in the forthcoming season.

First reproduction in this species, defined as the laying of the first clutch of eggs, occurs at 438 days since birth [tR = 438 days since birth] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that integrates the time needed for maturation, territory acquisition, and pair formation. The delay between reaching puberty and initiating a first brood is a common pattern among small passerines, reflecting the additional time required to secure a suitable nesting site and establish a stable pair bond. Females typically produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing two eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing two eggs], a modest reproductive output that is nevertheless typical for a bird of this size inhabiting a seasonally unpredictable environment. This annual reproductive effort represents a significant energetic investment for the female, who must accumulate sufficient nutrient reserves before laying the eggs and then share incubation duties with her mate. The combination of a low clutch size and a single annual breeding attempt suggests that the species employs a conservative life-history strategy, prioritizing adult survival over maximal fecundity in each season.

The physiological underpinnings of these life-history traits are reflected in the species' metabolic rate, measured under basal conditions. Respirometry trials revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 47.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 47.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at the standard thermoneutral temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that aligns closely with allometric predictions for a bird of its adult body mass. Females in the population attain an ultimate wet weight of 14.7 grams [Wwi = 14.7 grams], which represents the asymptotic mass reached after the completion of skeletal growth and the deposition of reproductive tissues. The high mass-specific metabolic rate is a correlate of the species' fast-paced early development and short generation time, demanding a continuous high intake of arthropod prey. Despite this elevated energy expenditure, the maximum lifespan recorded in the wild is 8 years [am = 8 years], indicating that the high metabolic throughput does not necessarily translate into accelerated senescence in this lineage at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Long-term banding studies have confirmed that some individuals survive for nearly a decade in their riparian habitats, although annual survival rates are low and most mortality occurs during the first year of life.
